Professional sanctions in AI hallucination cases

Group members: Ishita Jain, Ahlam Negash, Abigail Minin

GitHub repository: View our GitHub repository

Partner 1: Ishita Jain — research question, exploratory analysis, decision tree.

Partner 2: random forest, comparison, conclusions (name to be confirmed).

Partner 1: Research question

Can party type, jurisdiction, AI-tool identification, and primary legal field classify whether a documented AI hallucination case records a professional sanction? The response is Professional Sanction, with Yes as the positive class. This replaces the starter’s question about counts over time to meet the assignment’s classification requirement.

The data come from Damien Charlotin’s AI Hallucination Cases Database. Each row represents a documented case, not a randomly sampled use of AI. We predict the recorded label; No does not rule out later sanctions.

Partner 1: Exploratory analysis

cases <- read_csv("data/hallucination_cases.csv")
knitr::kable(cases |> count(`Professional Sanction`, name = "Cases"))
Professional Sanction Cases
No 1915
Yes 163 
model_data <- cases |>
  filter(`Professional Sanction` %in% c("No", "Yes")) |>
  transmute(
    sanction = factor(`Professional Sanction`, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    party = case_when(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(coalesce(`Party(ies)`, "")), "lawyer|prosecutor|defender") ~ "Lawyer involved",
      str_detect(str_to_lower(coalesce(`Party(ies)`, "")), "pro se") ~ "Pro se litigant",
      is.na(`Party(ies)`) ~ "Unknown",
      TRUE ~ "Other party"),
    jurisdiction = case_when(`State(s)` == "USA" ~ "USA",
                             is.na(`State(s)`) ~ "Unknown", TRUE ~ "Outside USA"),
    tool = case_when(str_to_lower(`AI Tool`) == "chatgpt" ~ "ChatGPT",
                    str_to_lower(`AI Tool`) %in% c("implied", "unidentified") | is.na(`AI Tool`) ~ "Unspecified or implied",
                    TRUE ~ "Other named tool"),
    legal_field = coalesce(`Legal Field Primary`, "Unknown"))
sanction_rate <- mean(model_data$sanction == "Yes")
ggplot(model_data, aes(sanction)) + geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Recorded professional sanction", y = "Cases",
       title = "Professional sanctions are uncommon") + theme_minimal()
party_summary <- model_data |> group_by(party) |>
  summarise(Cases = n(), Yes = sum(sanction == "Yes"),
            Sanction_rate = mean(sanction == "Yes"), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(party_summary, digits = 3)
party Cases Yes Sanction_rate
Lawyer involved 835 159 0.190
Other party 43 2 0.047
Pro se litigant 1194 2 0.002
Unknown 6 0 0.000 
ggplot(party_summary, aes(reorder(party, Sanction_rate), Sanction_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") + coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Party category", y = "Proportion with sanction",
       title = "Recorded sanction rates by party type") + theme_minimal()

There are 2078 cases; 0 are excluded for missing or unrecognized responses. Among retained cases, 7.84% record a sanction. The imbalanced response means high accuracy can conceal poor detection of Yes cases. The party chart compares rates rather than counts to account for category sizes. Lawyer involvement may be informative because professional discipline applies to legal professionals. These associations do not establish causation.

Shared modeling setup

set.seed(154)
train_id <- sample(seq_len(nrow(model_data)), round(0.7 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data[train_id, ]
test <- model_data[-train_id, ]
# Learn common fields from training data only; group unseen test levels.
common_fields <- train |> count(legal_field, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |> pull(legal_field)
prepare_predictors <- function(d) {
  d |> mutate(
    legal_field = factor(ifelse(legal_field %in% common_fields, legal_field, "Other"),
                         levels = c(common_fields, "Other")),
    party = factor(party, levels = c("Lawyer involved", "Pro se litigant", "Other party", "Unknown")),
    jurisdiction = factor(jurisdiction, levels = c("USA", "Outside USA", "Unknown")),
    tool = factor(tool, levels = c("ChatGPT", "Unspecified or implied", "Other named tool")))
}
train <- prepare_predictors(train)
test <- prepare_predictors(test)
model_formula <- sanction ~ party + jurisdiction + tool + legal_field
knitr::kable(data.frame(Set = c("Training", "Test"),
                       Cases = c(nrow(train), nrow(test)),
                       Yes_rate = c(mean(train$sanction == "Yes"), mean(test$sanction == "Yes"))), digits = 3)
Set Cases Yes_rate
Training 1455 0.080
Test 623 0.074

The seed-154 70/30 split gives 1455 training and 623 test cases. Partner 2 must reuse these processed sets and model_formula. Outcome text, monetary penalties, and case narratives are excluded because they could reveal the response; names and source links are also excluded. This is a retrospective random holdout, not a forecast of future cases.

The tree reduces Gini impurity to create more homogeneous sanction groups. The exploratory tree uses a prespecified CP of 0.001 and has 7 terminal nodes. Training-only ten-fold cross-validation instead selects CP = 0.01197, yielding 1 terminal nodes. Its preference for a single-node tree shows that these splits do not improve cross-validated overall error enough to justify their complexity. We interpret the larger tree as exploratory; the test set does not choose its settings. The first split uses party. The table shows its routing rules and the training sanction proportions on each side. The child with the larger Yes probability records sanctions more often.

One terminal node follows party=Pro se litigant,Other party,Unknown. It predicts No, with estimated Yes probability 0.002. This is a training-node proportion, not certainty about an individual case.

Partner 1: Held-out performance

classification_metrics <- function(prediction, actual) {
  cm <- table(Predicted = factor(prediction, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
              Actual = factor(actual, levels = c("No", "Yes")))
  sensitivity <- cm["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(cm[, "Yes"])
  specificity <- cm["No", "No"] / sum(cm[, "No"])
  c(Accuracy = sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm), Error = 1 - sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm),
    Sensitivity = sensitivity, Specificity = specificity,
    Balanced_accuracy = mean(c(sensitivity, specificity)))
}
tree_prob <- predict(tree_model, test, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
tree_class <- factor(ifelse(tree_prob >= 0.5, "Yes", "No"), levels = c("No", "Yes"))
tree_cm <- table(Predicted = tree_class, Actual = test$sanction)
tree_cm
         Actual
Predicted  No Yes
      No  572  41
      Yes   5   5
tree_metrics <- classification_metrics(tree_class, test$sanction)
baseline_metrics <- classification_metrics(rep("No", nrow(test)), test$sanction)
knitr::kable(rbind(Decision_tree = tree_metrics, Always_No = baseline_metrics), digits = 3)
Accuracy Error Sensitivity Specificity Balanced_accuracy
Decision_tree 0.926 0.074 0.109 0.991 0.55
Always_No 0.926 0.074 0.000 1.000 0.50

At a 0.5 Yes-probability cutoff, test accuracy is 92.62%, versus 92.62% for always predicting No. Sensitivity is 10.87%: the proportion of recorded Yes cases correctly identified. Specificity is 99.13%, the proportion of recorded No cases correctly identified. Balanced accuracy is 55%, giving both classes equal weight.

The cross-validation result favors the majority-class baseline over a complex tree, so the exploratory splits should not be treated as a validated improvement. The confusion matrix and sensitivity are essential because predicting No can yield high accuracy. The tree gives readable rules, but rare positives and small leaves can limit reliable detection. Reporting practices, different jurisdictional rules, and later changes in outcomes limit these results. Related cases or repeated parties can make a random holdout more optimistic than prediction for entirely new parties. These results describe this database, not sanction rates among all filings or causal effects of AI tools.
